title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine which, on every finite simplicial complex K promised to be a closed combinatorial 4-manifold, halts and decides whether K is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the boundary of a 5-simplex?
definitions: A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite family of finite vertex sets closed under taking subsets; its maximal sets are its facets. The input lists all facets with integer vertex labels in binary. K is pure of dimension 4 when all facets have five vertices. The link of a vertex v consists of the faces \(\sigma\) not containing v for which \(\sigma \cup \{v\}\) is a face of K. A closed combinatorial 4-manifold here is a nonempty pure 4-dimensional complex in which each vertex link is a PL 3-sphere; connectedness is not promised. The standard PL d-sphere is the boundary complex of a \((d+1)\)-simplex. Two complexes are PL homeomorphic when they admit finite simplicial subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic, equivalently when their geometric realizations admit a homeomorphism affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions. A simplicial subdivision triangulates the same realization by smaller simplices contained in the old simplices. Correctness and termination are required on every promised input; no behavior is required on other inputs. There is no time or space bound beyond termination.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
why: Locate the remaining decidability boundary for recognizing spheres in the piecewise-linear category.

importance.reason: A longstanding and precisely isolated computational-topology problem connecting finite combinatorial input with fundamental four-dimensional topology.

references.title: Applied topology: sphere recognition research presentation
Is there an algorithm to recognize the combinatorial four-sphere?

progress.text: The computational study distinguishes recognizing the standard PL sphere from detecting a topological sphere and reports inconclusive four-dimensional instances.
The research presentation retains dimension four as the unresolved recognition boundary.

context_blocks.text: A triangulation is finite data, but deciding the global space it describes may exceed the power of every algorithm. Sphere recognition is decidable in low dimensions and undecidable from dimension five onward; dimension four is the exceptional unresolved case in this PL formulation.

The category matters: a topological homeomorphism need not supply a PL equivalence. The practical study explicitly distinguishes a homology four-sphere, a topological four-sphere and the standard PL four-sphere. This card asks for recognition of the last object.

Successful recognition on large test collections does not establish termination on every promised manifold. The question is about the existence of a decision procedure, rather than the speed or reliability of a particular implementation.

sentences: The input is a finite triangulation promised to be a closed combinatorial four-dimensional manifold.
The task is to recognize the standard piecewise-linear four-sphere.
The question asks for a terminating decision algorithm, with no polynomial-time requirement.
Recognizing a topological sphere or checking its homology would answer a different question.
The problem marks the exceptional dimension between established decidability and undecidability results for sphere recognition.
